title: 05. Load Balancing & Scalability: Layer 7 Load Balancer
summary: A Layer 7 load balancer operates at the OSI application layer (HTTP/HTTPS, gRPC, HTTP/2), inspecting the full request — method, URL, headers, cookies, body — to make content-aware routing decisions, terminate TLS, rewrite…
objectives: What can a Layer 7 load balancer see and do that a Layer 4 balancer cannot?
What is TLS termination, and why is it almost always done at the L7 balancer rather than at backends?
How does an L7 balancer implement sticky sessions, and why would you use (or avoid) them?
What is the difference between path-based routing and host-based routing, and when do you combine them?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A Layer 7 load balancer operates at the OSI application layer (HTTP/HTTPS, gRPC, HTTP/2), inspecting the full request — method, URL, headers, cookies, body — to make content-aware routing decisions, terminate TLS, rewrite headers, and apply policies that are invisible to a Layer 4 balancer.

A Layer 7 (L7) load balancer terminates the client's TCP connection, parses the application-layer protocol (HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, HTTP/2, HTTP/3), and makes a routing decision based on the full content of the request — URL path, host header, cookies, query parameters, custom headers, even the request body. Only then does it open a new TCP connection to the chosen backend and forward the request, possibly rewriting headers, terminating TLS, or compressing the response along the way. The benefit is precision: an L7 balancer can route `/api/v1/users/*` to the user-service backend, `/api/v1/payments/*` to the payments-service backend, and `/static/*` to a CDN-origin backend — all from one VIP, all from one DNS name. The cost is parsing overhead: every request must be fully received and decoded before a routing decision can be made, which makes L7 inherently slower than L4 per-connection but vastly more flexible per-request.

The **first** reason L7 dominates modern web architectures is **content-based routing**. A typical microservice backend has dozens of services — user, billing, catalog, search, recommendation, chat, notifications — each with its own deployment, scaling, and version. Without L7, you'd need a separate VIP, DNS name, and certificate for each, multiplying operational overhead. With L7, you expose one hostname (`api.example.com`) and route by URL path: `/users/*` to user-service, `/billing/*` to billing-service, and so on. AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) operationalizes this with **listener rules** — match on path, host, HTTP header, or query string, then route to a target group. NGINX does the same with `location` blocks. Envoy does it with `route_config` and HTTP route matchers. Netflix's Zuul gateway, an L7 load balancer built on Netty, routes Netflix's entire API surface through one hostname with hundreds of path-based rules — the kind of consolidation that would be impossible at L4.

The **second** reason is **TLS termination**. HTTPS is now ubiquitous, and terminating TLS at the load balancer — decrypting the incoming stream, handling the certificate, then talking plaintext HTTP to the backend (or re-encrypting if the network is untrusted) — is the standard pattern. The benefit: certificates live in one place (the balancer), cert rotation is centralized, backends don't waste CPU on crypto, and the balancer can inspect the decrypted traffic for routing, logging, and WAF rules. AWS ALB integrates with AWS Certificate Manager for automatic cert provisioning and renewal; NGINX uses `ssl_certificate` directives; Envoy uses SDS (Secret Discovery Service) for dynamic cert injection. The trade-off: the balancer becomes a crypto bottleneck under high TLS load, which is why high-throughput sites use dedicated TLS-termination fleets (Netflix's Zuul does TLS at the edge with hardware-accelerated crypto) or split L4/L7 tiers (NLB for raw throughput, ALB behind for HTTP logic). End-to-end TLS — where the balancer passes encrypted bytes through without decryption — is the alternative when compliance requires it (HIPAA, PCI in some interpretations), but loses the routing and observability benefits.

The **third** reason is **request transformation**. An L7 balancer can rewrite headers (`X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto`), inject cookies (sticky session affinity), strip headers (security: remove internal `X-Debug-*` from outbound), compress responses (gzip, br), cache responses (NGINX's `proxy_cache`, Varnish), and even modify the request body. This is invaluable for legacy integration — adding an auth header for backends that don't validate tokens themselves, rewriting old API paths to new ones during a migration, or injecting a request ID for distributed tracing. NGINX's `proxy_set_header` is the textbook example; Envoy's Lua and WASM filters go further, allowing arbitrary logic. AWS ALB's built-in `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` injection is what lets backends know the original client IP and scheme despite sitting behind a balancer that terminates the connection — without these headers, every backend would see the balancer's IP in its access logs, breaking geo-blocking, rate-limiting, and audit.

The **fourth** reason is **protocol-level features**. L7 balancers understand HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC) and can translate between them — accept HTTP/3 from clients, talk HTTP/1.1 to legacy backends, multiplex many client streams onto fewer backend connections. They understand gRPC and can route by gRPC method (package.service/method), enabling per-method routing and rate limiting. They understand WebSocket upgrades and handle them natively. They can do per-request retries with backoff, circuit breaking, and outlier detection — features that L4 simply cannot offer because they require inspecting the response. Envoy is the canonical feature-rich L7 — built by Lyft, adopted by Istio, AWS App Mesh, and most service meshes — because its filter chain lets you compose auth, rate-limit, tracing, retry, and routing logic per request.

Real-world examples are extensive. **AWS ALB** is the managed default — path/host/header/query routing, TLS termination, integration with ACM, native WebSocket and HTTP/2 support, used by the majority of AWS-hosted web services. **NGINX** is the open-source standard — Netflix's edge, Airbnb's front door, Cloudflare's per-customer config — configured via `nginx.conf`, runs as a reverse proxy and load balancer, supports Lua for custom logic. **HAProxy in HTTP mode** is the high-performance choice — Airbnb uses it, Cloudflare uses it for some layers, it can hit hundreds of thousands of HTTPS requests per second per box. **Envoy** is the modern dynamic choice — Lyft, Uber, Stripe, and most service-mesh adopters — configured via xDS APIs, hot-reloads without dropping connections, and is the data plane for Istio, Consul Connect, and AWS App Mesh. **Google's GFE (Google Front End)** is Google's in-house L7 — fronts every Google HTTP service, terminates TLS, applies security policies, and is the foundation of Google Cloud Load Balancing. **Traefik** and **Caddy** are the cloud-native newcomers — auto-configured from container labels and Kubernetes ingress, popular for developer ergonomics.

The trade-offs of L7 are real. **Latency**: parsing HTTP adds microseconds-to-milliseconds per request, and TLS termination adds crypto overhead — typically 1–5 ms per request, which matters at p99. **Throughput ceiling**: an L7 balancer tops out at hundreds of thousands of RPS per box, vs. millions of connections per second for L4. **Connection management**: the balancer must maintain two connection pools (client-side and backend-side), doubling the file-descriptor and memory pressure. **Failure modes**: an L7 balancer crash drops in-flight requests mid-parse, and HTTP-level timeouts (header timeout, body timeout, idle timeout) can cause subtle failures if misconfigured. **Operational complexity**: routing rules, header rewrites, and TLS configs become a sprawling codebase that needs version control, CI, and rollback — the rise of GitOps for LB config (Terraform for AWS ALB, Crossplane, Argo CD for Kubernetes Ingress) is a direct response. These trade-offs are why L4 and L7 coexist in nearly every production architecture: L4 for raw throughput at the edge, L7 for content logic one hop behind. The decision is rarely "L4 or L7" — it is "where do we put each."

Terminate TLS (decrypt) | | 2. Parse HTTP request | | method=GET path=/api/v1/.. | | headers, cookies | | 3. Match listener rules | | 4. Pick target group | | 5. Inject X-Forwarded-* | | 6. Open new conn to backend | | 7. Forward request | +---------------------------------+ | | | | v v v v +------+ +-------+ +-----+ +-------+ | /api | | /api | | /st | | Host: | | /v1/ | | /v1/ | | atic| | admin | | users| | pay | | | | | +------+ +-------+ +-----+ +-------+ | | | | v v v v user-svc pay-svc cdn-orig admin-svc (3 pods) (2 pods) (5 pods) (1 pod) Routing rules an L7 can match (L4 can match NONE of these): path: /api/* /static/* /healthz host: api.example.com vs www.example.com header: X-Api-Version: 2 query: ?preview=true cookie: session_id=abc123 (sticky) method: GET vs POST body: content-type=application/json (rare) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The client opens a TLS connection to the L7 balancer's VIP and sends `GET /api/v1/users/42` with headers and cookies. The balancer terminates TLS — decrypts the stream using its certificate, validates the SNI, and now has plaintext HTTP bytes. 2. The balancer parses the HTTP request fully — method, path, host header, query string, cookies, custom headers. This parsing is what enables content-aware routing; it is also the per-request overhead that makes L7 slower than L4. 3. The balancer consults its listener rules (priority-ordered) and finds the first match — e.g., "path starts with `/api/v1/users/` → target group `user-service`." It picks a backend from that target group using a load-balancing algorithm (round-robin, least-outstanding-requests). 4. Before forwarding, the balancer injects headers: `X-Forwarded-For: `, `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, `X-Request-ID: ` for tracing. If sticky sessions are enabled, it may also set a `Set-Cookie` so the next request from this client lands on the same backend. 5. The balancer opens a new TCP connection to the backend (plaintext HTTP, or re-encrypted HTTPS if required), sends the request, receives the response, and forwards it to the client — optionally caching, compressing, or transforming it along the way. Per-request features like retries, circuit breaking, and outlier detection apply because the balancer can see HTTP status codes and latencies.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Routes HTTP requests to target groups based on URL path.
- Layer 7 HTTP load balancer with content-based routing.
- Demonstrates: path-based routing, header injection, sticky sessions,
- Per-target-group algorithms. Built on Python's http.server + urllib.
- Ordered list of (path_prefix, target_group) rules
- Sort longest-prefix-first so /api/v1/users wins over /api
- If client has a sticky cookie pointing at a healthy backend, reuse it.
- Otherwise pick fresh and set a cookie

**Defines:** `Backend`, `TargetGroup`, `Layer7LoadBalancer`, `Handler`

```python
# Layer 7 HTTP load balancer with content-based routing.
# Demonstrates: path-based routing, header injection, sticky sessions,
# per-target-group algorithms. Built on Python's http.server + urllib.

import http.server
import json
import socketserver
import threading
import urllib.request
import urllib.error
import uuid
import time
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Backend:
    url: str                          # e.g. "http://10.0.1.5:8080"
    healthy: bool = True
    inflight: int = 0
    _lock: threading.Lock = field(default_factory=threading.Lock)

@dataclass
class TargetGroup:
    name: str
    backends: list[Backend]
    algorithm: str = "round_robin"     # or "least_inflight"
    _idx: int = 0
    _lock: threading.Lock = field(default_factory=threading.Lock)

    def pick(self) -> Backend | None:
        healthy = [b for b in self.backends if b.healthy]
        if not healthy:
            return None
        if self.algorithm == "least_inflight":
            return min(healthy, key=lambda b: b.inflight)
        # round robin
        with self._lock:
            b = healthy[self._idx % len(healthy)]
            self._idx += 1
        return b

class Layer7LoadBalancer:
    """Routes HTTP requests to target groups based on URL path."""

    def __init__(self, port: int = 8080):
        self.port = port
        # Ordered list of (path_prefix, target_group) rules
        self.rules: list[tuple[str, TargetGroup]] = []
        self.sticky_sessions: dict[str, Backend] = {}   # cookie -> backend
        self._sticky_lock = threading.Lock()

    def add_rule(self, path_prefix: str, tg: TargetGroup):
        self.rules.append((path_prefix, tg))
        # Sort longest-prefix-first so /api/v1/users wins over /api
        self.rules.sort(key=lambda r: len(r[0]), reverse=True)

    def _match_target_group(self, path: str) -> TargetGroup | None:
        for prefix, tg in self.rules:
            if path.startswith(prefix):
                return tg
        return None

    def _pick_with_stickiness(self, tg: TargetGroup, cookies: str) -> Backend | None:
        # If client has a sticky cookie pointing at a healthy backend, reuse it.
        if cookies:
            for c in cookies.split(";"):
                if "L7STICKY=" in c:
                    cookie = c.split("=", 1)[1].strip()
                    with self._sticky_lock:
                        b = self.sticky_sessions.get(cookie)
                    if b and b.healthy:
                        return b
        # Otherwise pick fresh and set a cookie
        b = tg.pick()
        if b is not None:
            cookie = uuid.uuid4().hex
            with self._sticky_lock:
                self.sticky_sessions[cookie] = b
            b._sticky_cookie = cookie   # stash for response header
        return b

    def handle(self, method, path, headers, body):
        tg = self._match_target_group(path)
        if tg is None:
            return (404, {"Content-Type": "text/plain"}, b"no route matches " + path.encode())

        backend = self._pick_with_stickiness(tg, headers.get("Cookie", ""))
        if backend is None:
            return (503, {"Content-Type": "text/plain"}, b"no healthy backends in " + tg.name.encode())

        # Inject L7 headers so backend sees the original client
        fwd_headers = dict(headers)
        fwd_headers["X-Forwarded-For"] = headers.get("X-Forwarded-For", "127.0.0.1")
        fwd_headers["X-Forwarded-Proto"] = "https"
        fwd_headers["X-Request-ID"] = uuid.uuid4().hex

        with backend._lock:
            backend.inflight += 1
        try:
            url = backend.url.rstrip("/") + path
            req = urllib.request.Request(url, data=body, method=method, headers=fwd_headers)
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5) as resp:
                status = resp.status
                resp_headers = dict(resp.headers)
                resp_body = resp.read()
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            status, resp_headers, resp_body = e.code, dict(e.headers), e.read()
        except Exception as e:
            backend.healthy = False
            return (502, {"Content-Type": "text/plain"}, f"backend error: {e}".encode())
        finally:
            with backend._lock:
                backend.inflight -= 1

        # Attach sticky cookie if we created one
        if hasattr(backend, "_sticky_cookie"):
            resp_headers["Set-Cookie"] = f"L7STICKY={backend._sticky_cookie}; Path=/"
            del backend._sticky_cookie

        return (status, resp_headers, resp_body)

class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    lb: Layer7LoadBalancer = None     # injected at runtime

    def _serve(self):
        body = b""
        if self.command in ("POST", "PUT", "PATCH"):
            length = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", 0))
            body = self.rfile.read(length) if length else b""
        status, headers, body_out = self.lb.handle(self.command, self.path,
                                                   dict(self.headers), body)
        self.send_response(status)
        for k, v in headers.items():
            self.send_header(k, v)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body_out)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body_out)

    # Route all methods through the same handler
    do_GET = do_POST = do_PUT = do_DELETE = do_PATCH = _serve

if __name__ == "__main__":
    lb = Layer7LoadBalancer(port=8080)
    lb.add_rule("/api/v1/users",    TargetGroup("users",    [Backend("http://127.0.0.1:9001"),
                                                            Backend("http://127.0.0.1:9002")]))
    lb.add_rule("/api/v1/payments", TargetGroup("payments", [Backend("http://127.0.0.1:9101")]))
    lb.add_rule("/static",          TargetGroup("static",   [Backend("http://127.0.0.1:9201")]))

    Handler.lb = lb
    with socketserver.ThreadingTCPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8080), Handler) as httpd:
        print(f"[L7] listening on 0.0.0.0:8080 with {len(lb.rules)} routes")
        httpd.serve_forever()
```

quiz.explanation: An L7 balancer can inspect the full application-layer request — HTTP method, URL path, host header, query string, cookies, custom headers, and (in some cases) request body — and route based on any of these.

quiz.question: How does an L7 balancer implement sticky sessions, and why would you use (or avoid) them?
options: The problem is config-as-monolith — one file owned by everyone is no one's, and changes conflict.
Envoy has rich observability built in — start with the admin endpoint /stats (or Prometheus metrics scraped via the stats sink).
Use the strangler-fig pattern with an L7 balancer (ALB or NGINX) doing path-based routing.
Sticky sessions (session affinity) route requests from the same client to the same backend, preserving per-client state across requests.
quiz.explanation: Sticky sessions (session affinity) route requests from the same client to the same backend, preserving per-client state across requests. L7 implements this by setting a cookie on the first response — either an application cookie (e.g., JSESSIONID, which the balancer learns to track) or a balancer-generated cookie (e.g., AWS ALB's AWSALB cookie, encoded with the target ID).

quiz.question: What is the difference between path-based routing and host-based routing, and when do you combine them?
options: These features dramatically improve reliability: a single bad backend cannot drag down the fleet because outlier detection ejects it; transient network blips don't reach the user because…

quiz.explanation: Path-based routing matches on the URL path — /api/v1/users/* to one target, /api/v1/payments/* to another, /static/* to a CDN-origin backend — all from the same hostname. Host-based routing matches on the Host header — api.example.com to one target group, www.example.com to another, admin.example.com to a third — all from the same VIP and listener. AWS ALB supports both, with host rules evaluated before path rules.
